en: Dīgha Nikāya 9:
Poṭṭhapādasutta 1.
The Account of the Wanderer Poṭṭhapāda
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now at that time the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda was residing at Mallikā’s Park, a single-hall *tinduka*-grove for those who debate various doctrines, together with a large assembly of wanderers, about three hundred wanderers in all.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī."
"What if I were to go to Mallikā’s park, the Samayappavādaka Tindukācīra with its single sala tree, where the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda is?
Then the Blessed One went to Mallikā’s park, the Samayappavādaka Tindukācīra with its single sala tree.
Now at that time, the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda was seated together with a large assembly of wanderers, who were making a great clamor and loud noise, discussing various kinds of trivial talk.
That is to say: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers,
talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks, talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of scents, talk of relatives,
talk of vehicles, talk of villages, talk of towns, talk of cities, talk of districts, talk of women, and talk of heroes.
[They were engaged in] talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about ancestors, various kinds of talk, talk about the world, talk about the ocean,
talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be," or such like.
Then the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen them, he settled his own assembly, saying:
"Be quiet, sirs; do not make a noise, sirs.
This ascetic Gotama is coming."
"That venerable one is fond of quietude and speaks in praise of quietude.
Perhaps, having perceived a quiet assembly, he might think it fit to approach.
When this was said, those wanderers became silent.
Then the Blessed One approached the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda.
Then the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda said this to the Blessed One:
"Let the Blessed One come, venerable sir."
“Welcome, Bhante, to the Blessed One.
It has been long, Bhante, since the Blessed One made this occasion to come here.
Let the Blessed One sit down; this seat is prepared.”
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The wanderer Poṭṭhapāda also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Poṭṭhapāda, for what discussion have you been sitting together here now, and what was the conversation of yours that was left unfinished?

When this was said, the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda addressed the Blessed One as follows: 1.1. Discussion on the Cessation of Perception [The wanderers replied: “We were sitting together here, venerable sir, discussing the cessation of perception. [The Blessed One asked: “And what, Poṭṭhapāda, was the conversation of yours that was left unfinished? Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer spoke thus to the Blessed One: [and related the discussion].
“Let this discussion, venerable sir, stand for now—the discussion for which we are currently seated together.
This discussion, venerable sir, will not be difficult for the Blessed One to hear at a later time as well.

Venerable sir, in former days, even earlier than that, when various ascetics and brahmins of other sects were seated and assembled in the Hall of Wonders, a discussion arose concerning the cessation of perception.”
‘How, sir, does the cessation of perception come about?
On this point, some said:
‘The perceptions of a person arise and cease without cause and without condition.’
‘At whatever time they arise, at that time one is percipient;
at whatever time they cease, at that time one is non-percipient.
In this way, some proclaim the cessation of perception.
Another said this to him:
“But that cannot be so, sir.
For perception, sir, is a person’s self.”
"And it is indeed that [consciousness] which enters and departs.
At the time when it enters, one is percipient;
at the time when it departs, one is non-percipient."
Some proclaim the cessation of perception.
Another says this to him:
"But that cannot be so, sir."
For there are, sir, recluses and brahmins of great psychic power and great majesty who can draw perception toward this person and draw it away from him.
At whatever time they draw it toward him, at that time he possesses perception.
‘At the time when they pull him out, at that time he is non-percipient.
Thus some proclaim the cessation of perception.
Regarding this, another says:
"But this will not be so, sir.
For there are deities, sir, of great power and great majesty;
they draw the perception of this man toward them, or draw it away from them."
‘At the time when they pull [him] toward [it], at that time he is percipient;
at the time when they pull [him] away [from it], at that time he is non-percipient.
In this way, some proclaim the cessation of perception.
Then, venerable sir, mindfulness arose in me concerning the Blessed One himself:
"Oh, how skilled the Blessed One is! Oh, how well-gone is the Sugata, who is so thoroughly proficient in these teachings!
Venerable sir, the Blessed One is skilled; the Blessed One is one who knows the way things are regarding the cessation of perception.
“Venerable sir, how does the cessation of perception come about?
“In this regard, Poṭṭhapāda, as for those recluses and brahmins who say: ‘... [this is] the discourse on the arising and cessation of perception together with its cause.”
‘Perceptions arise and cease in a person without cause and without condition’—from the very beginning they have failed in this. And why?
Because, Poṭṭhapāda, perceptions arise and cease in a person with a cause and with a condition.
“One perception arises through training, and one perception ceases through training.
And what is that training? Thus the Blessed One spoke.
“In this case, Poṭṭhapāda, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One … [as in the standard formula] …”
In this way, Poṭṭhapāda, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue … [as before] … When he sees within himself that these five hindrances have been abandoned, gladness arises;

in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, he experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.

Thus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
His former perception of sensual pleasures ceases.

At that time, there is a subtle and true perception of the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; at that time, he possesses precisely that subtle and true perception of the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
Thus, through training, one perception arises and another perception ceases.
“This is the training,” the Blessed One said.

“Furthermore, Poṭṭhapāda, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
His former subtle and true perception of the rapture and happiness born of seclusion ceases.”

"At that time there is the subtle and true perception of rapture and pleasure born of concentration; at that time one possesses only the subtle and true perception of rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
In this way, with training, one perception arises and another perception ceases.
This too is training," the Blessed One said.
“Furthermore, Poṭṭhapāda, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness’;
thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
His former subtle and true perception of rapture and pleasure born of concentration ceases.
At that time, there is a subtle and true perception of equanimity and pleasure; at that time, he possesses only that subtle and true perception of equanimity and pleasure.
Thus, with training, one perception arises and, with training, another perception ceases.
“This too is a training,” the Blessed One said.
“Furthermore, Poṭṭhapāda, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.”
He enters and dwells in that jhāna.
His previous perception of subtle truth consisting of equanimity and pleasure ceases.
At that time, there is a perception of subtle truth consisting of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; at that time, he possesses precisely that perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
“In this way too, Poṭṭhapāda, one training gives rise to a certain perception, and another training ceases that perception.
This too is training,” the Blessed One said.

“Furthermore, Poṭṭhapāda, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.”
His previous perception of form ceases.
At that time, there is the subtle and true perception of the base of infinite space; at that time, he possesses only the subtle and true perception of the base of infinite space.
Thus, in training, one perception arises and another perception ceases.
“This too is a training,” the Blessed One said.
“Furthermore, Poṭṭhapāda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
His former subtle and true perception of the base of infinite space ceases.”
"At that time there is a subtle and true perception of the base of infinite consciousness; at that time one is indeed possessed of a subtle and true perception of the base of infinite consciousness.
Thus, with this training, one perception arises and another perception ceases.
This too is training," so said the Blessed One.
“Furthermore, Poṭṭhapāda, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [a bhikkhu] enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, [perceiving]: ‘There is nothing.
His former subtle and true perception of the base of infinite consciousness ceases.
At that time, there is the subtle and true perception of the base of nothingness; at that time, he possesses only the subtle and true perception of the base of nothingness.”
“Thus too, Poṭṭhapāda, one perception arises through training, and another perception ceases through training.
This too is training,” the Blessed One said.
“When, Poṭṭhapāda, a bhikkhu here possesses his own perception, he then, from there to there, gradually touches the peak of perception.”
As he stands at the peak of perception, it occurs to him:
"For one who intends, it is worse; for one who does not intend, it is better.
But if I were to intend and form a mental formation, these perceptions of mine would cease, and other, coarser perceptions would arise."
"What if I were neither to intend nor to form a volitional formation?
He neither intends nor forms a volitional formation.
As he does not intend and does not form a volitional formation, those very perceptions cease, and no other coarse perceptions arise.
Thus one touches cessation.
In this way, Poṭṭhapāda, there is the attainment of the progressive cessation of perception with full awareness.
What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda?
“Have you ever heard before of such gradual attainment of the cessation of perception while possessing full awareness?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
It is in this way, Bhante, that I understand the Blessed One’s teaching:”
“Poṭṭhapāda, when a bhikkhu here possesses his own perception, he passes from there to there, and from there to there, gradually touching the peak of perception.
While standing at the peak of perception, it occurs to him:
‘For one who intends, it is worse; for one who does not intend, it is better.’”
"If I were to think and form an intention, these perceptions of mine would cease and other grosser perceptions would arise;
what if I were neither to think nor to form an intention?
He neither thought nor formed an intention. As he did not think and did not form an intention, those very perceptions ceased and other grosser perceptions did not arise.
“Thus one touches cessation.
In this way, Poṭṭhapāda, there is the attainment of the progressive cessation of perception with full awareness.
“It is so, Poṭṭhapāda.”
“Venerable sir, does the Blessed One prescribe only one pinnacle of perception, or does he prescribe many pinnacles of perception?
“Poṭṭhapāda, I prescribe one pinnacle of perception, and I also prescribe many pinnacles of perception.
“But in what way, venerable sir, does the Blessed One prescribe one pinnacle of perception, and in what way does he prescribe many pinnacles of perception?”
“In whatever way, Poṭṭhapāda, one touches cessation, in that way I describe the pinnacle of perception.
It is in this way, Poṭṭhapāda, that I describe both a single pinnacle of perception and many pinnacles of perception.

“Venerable sir, does perception arise first and knowledge afterwards; or does knowledge arise first and perception afterwards; or do perception and knowledge arise neither before nor after each other?”
“Perception, Poṭṭhapāda, arises first, and knowledge arises later; with the arising of perception, there is the arising of knowledge.
He understands thus:
‘Indeed, it is due to this specific condition that my knowledge has arisen.’”
"By this method, Poṭṭhapāda, it should be understood how perception arises first and knowledge afterwards, and that with the arising of perception, there is the arising of knowledge.
1.3. The Discourse on Perception as Self (Saññā-attakathā)
“Venerable sir, is perception the self of a person, or is perception one thing and the self another?
“But what kind of self do you assume, Poṭṭhapāda?
“Venerable sir, I assume a gross self, material, composed of the four great elements, and sustained by solid food.”

“Moreover, Poṭṭhapāda, if your self were gross, material, composed of the four great elements, and nourished by physical food, then in that case, Poṭṭhapāda, your perception would be one thing and your self another.
By this method, Poṭṭhapāda, it should be understood how perception is one thing and the self is another.”
“Poṭṭhapāda, while this gross self—material, composed of the four great elements, and sustained by solid food—continues to exist, other perceptions arise for this person and other perceptions cease.
It is by this method, Poṭṭhapāda, that it should be understood how there will be one perception and another self.
“Venerable sir, I maintain that the self is mind-made, complete with all its limbs and faculties, and not lacking any sense organ.”

“Moreover, Poṭṭhapāda, if your self were mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, and possessed of unimpaired faculties, even so, Poṭṭhapāda, your perception would be one thing and your self another.
This can be understood by this method, Poṭṭhapāda, how perception is one thing and the self another:
while that mind-made self remains, complete in all its limbs and parts and possessed of unimpaired faculties, other perceptions arise for this person and other perceptions cease.”
"By this method also, Poṭṭhapāda, it should be understood that perception will be one thing and the self another.
"But, Bhante, I maintain that the self is formless and made of perception.
"If, Poṭṭhapāda, your self were formless and made of perception, even so, Poṭṭhapāda, perception would be one thing and the self another."
“By this method, Poṭṭhapāda, it should be understood that perception will be one thing and the self another.
For while this formless self consisting of perception remains constant, Poṭṭhapāda, other perceptions arise for this person and other perceptions cease.
By this method also, Poṭṭhapāda, it should be understood that perception will be one thing and the self another.”
“But is it possible for me, Bhante, to know this:
‘Perception is a person’s self,’ or ‘perception is one thing and the self is another’?
“Poṭṭhapāda, this is difficult for you to know—being of a different view, of a different inclination, of a different preference, engaged in a different practice, and following a different teacher.”
“‘Perception is the self of a person,’ or ‘perception is one thing and the self is another.

“If this, venerable sir, is difficult for me to understand— being of a different view, of a different inclination, of a different preference, engaged in a different practice, and following a different teacher—
as to whether ‘perception is the self of a person’ or ‘perception is one thing and the self is another’;”
“But what, venerable sir, about this: ‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’?
“Poṭṭhapāda, this has not been declared by me:
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.’”
“But, venerable sir, what about this: ‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’?
“Poṭṭhapāda, this too has been left undeclared by me:
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.’”
“But what, venerable sir, is the case regarding: ‘the world is finite’ … ‘the world is infinite’ … ‘the soul and the body are the same’ …”
‘The soul is one thing and the body another’ … ‘A Tathāgata exists after death’ … ‘A Tathāgata does not exist after death’ …
‘Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death… or does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolishness’?
“This too, Poṭṭhapāda, has been left undeclared by me:”
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish.
‘But why, Bhante, has this been left undeclared by the Blessed One?

‘Because this, Poṭṭhapāda, is not connected with the goal, not connected with the Dhamma, and does not pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life; it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna.’
“Therefore, Poṭṭhapāda, this was left undeclared by me.
“But what, Bhante, was declared by the Blessed One?
“‘This is suffering,’ Poṭṭhapāda, was declared by me. ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ Poṭṭhapāda, was declared by me.”
“I have declared it, Poṭṭhapāda. ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ Poṭṭhapāda, I have declared. ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ Poṭṭhapāda, I have declared.
“But why, Bhante, has this been declared by the Blessed One?”

“For this, Poṭṭhapāda, is connected with the goal, this is connected with the Dhamma, this pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life; it leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
Therefore, this has been declared by me.
“So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!”
“Venerable sir, let it be as the Blessed One deems it now the right time.
Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after the Blessed One had left, those wanderers began to revile Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer from all sides with verbal taunts and sharp reproaches.
“In exactly the same way, this venerable Poṭṭhapāda simply approves of whatever the ascetic Gotama says, saying:
‘So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
Yet we do not understand any categorical teaching of the Dhamma as taught by the ascetic Gotama.”

‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ or ‘the world is finite,’ or ‘the world is infinite,’ or ‘the soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ or ‘a Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’
‘Or does he exist after death? or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
When this was said, the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda said to those wanderers:
“I too, sirs, do not understand any categorical teaching given by the ascetic Gotama.”
‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ …pe… ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—
rather, the ascetic Gotama proclaims the real, the true, the suchness, the practice, the stability of phenomena, and the fixed order of phenomena.

“Indeed, for one who proclaims a practice that is real, true, and such as it is— the stability of phenomena and the fixed order of phenomena— how could a wise person like me not approve of what has been well-spoken by the ascetic Gotama?
Then, after two or three days had passed, Citta Hatthisāriputta and the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda [approached the Blessed One].
They approached the Blessed One. Having approached, Citta Hatthisāriputta paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
But the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda said this to the Blessed One:
“Then, venerable sir, not long after the Blessed One had departed, those wanderers surrounded me and assailed me with a torrent of words, saying:
‘In this very way, this worthy Poṭṭhapāda simply echoes whatever the ascetic Gotama says:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.”’”
Yet we do not understand any categorical teaching on the Dhamma from the ascetic Gotama, such as:
"The world is eternal," or "the world is not eternal"; "the world is finite," or "the world is infinite";
"the soul and the body are the same," or "the soul is one thing and the body another"; or "a Tathāgata exists after death..."

‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
When they had spoken thus, Bhante, I said this to those wanderers:
“Sir, I too do not understand any categorical teaching taught by the ascetic Gotama,
such as: ‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘The world is not eternal’ … [and so on] … or ‘A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
"Moreover, the ascetic Gotama proclaims a practice that is real, true, and such as it is—the stability of phenomena and the fixed order of phenomena.

Now, when one proclaims a practice that is real, true, and such as it is—the stability of phenomena and the fixed order of phenomena—how could a wise person like me not approve of what has been well-spoken by the ascetic Gotama?
"Poṭṭhapāda, all these wanderers are indeed blind and sightless."
You alone among them are the one with vision. For,
Poṭṭhapāda, I have taught and proclaimed some doctrines as having a single side,
and I have also taught and proclaimed other doctrines as not having a single side.
And what, Poṭṭhapāda, are those non-categorical teachings that have been taught and proclaimed by me?
"The world is eternal," Poṭṭhapāda, is a non-categorical teaching that has been taught and proclaimed by me;
"The world is not eternal," Poṭṭhapāda, is a non-categorical teaching that has been taught and proclaimed by me.
‘The world is finite,’ Poṭṭhapāda … ‘The world is infinite,’ Poṭṭhapāda … ‘The soul and the body are the same,’ Poṭṭhapāda …
‘The soul is one thing and the body another,’ Poṭṭhapāda… ‘A Tathāgata exists after death,’ Poṭṭhapāda… ‘A Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ Poṭṭhapāda…
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ Poṭṭhapāda—this, indeed, is a non-categorical teaching established by me.
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ Poṭṭhapāda—this, indeed, is a non-categorical teaching established by me.
And for what reason, Poṭṭhapāda, have these non-categorical teachings been taught and established by me?

"No, Poṭṭhapāda, those things are not connected with the goal, not connected with the Dhamma, not fundamental to the holy life, and they do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
Therefore, these indeterminate matters have been taught and declared by me.
2.1. Indeterminate Matters (Ekaṁsikadhammā)
And what, Poṭṭhapāda, are those categorical teachings that have been taught and proclaimed by me?
"This is suffering," Poṭṭhapāda, is a categorical teaching that has been taught and proclaimed by me.
"This is the origin of suffering," Poṭṭhapāda, is a categorical teaching that has been taught and proclaimed by me.
"This is the cessation of suffering," Poṭṭhapāda, this is the categorical Dhamma taught and proclaimed by me.
"This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," Poṭṭhapāda, this is the categorical Dhamma taught and proclaimed by me.
And why, Poṭṭhapāda, have these categorical Dharmas been taught and proclaimed by me?

For these, Poṭṭhapāda, are connected with the goal, connected with the Dhamma; they pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life and lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
Therefore, these categorical teachings have been taught and proclaimed by me.
There are, Poṭṭhapāda, some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘The self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death.
Having approached them, I say this:
‘Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a doctrine and such a view?’”
‘The self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death’?
If, when asked by me in this way, they admit,
“Yes,” then I say to them:
“But do you, venerable sirs, dwell knowing and seeing the world as exclusively pleasant?
When asked this, they say, “No. To them I say:
“But, venerable sirs, do you perceive yourselves as experiencing unalloyed happiness for one night or one day, or even for half a night or half a day?
When asked this, they say, “No. To them I say:
“But do you, venerable sirs, know:
‘This is the path, this is the way for the realization of an exclusively happy world’?
Being asked thus, they say, “No.”
I say this to them:
"But, venerable sirs, do you hear the voices of those deities who have been reborn in a world of exclusive happiness as they speak thus:
'You have practiced well, dear sirs; you have practiced straightly, dear sirs, for the realization of a world of exclusive happiness'?"
‘For we too, dear sir, having practiced in this way, have been reborn in a world of absolute happiness.
When asked thus, they say, ‘No.
What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda?
“But if this were so, would not the speech of those ascetics and brahmins turn out to be without foundation?
“Certainly, venerable sir, if this were so, the speech of those ascetics and brahmins would turn out to be without foundation.
“Suppose, Poṭṭhapāda, a man were to say this:”
‘I desire and long for her who is the most beautiful woman in this country.
Then they would say to him:
‘Good man, do you know whether that most beautiful woman in the country whom you desire and long for is a khattiya woman, a brahmin woman, a vessa woman, or a sudda woman?’”
Being asked thus, he would say, "No.
Then they would say to him:
"O man, do you know that most beautiful woman in the land whom you desire and lust after?"
‘Is he of such a name, or of such a clan; is he tall, or short, or of medium height; is he dark, or fair, or of golden complexion;
or does he live in such a village, town, or city?
Being asked thus, he would say, ‘No.’”
They would say to him:
“O man, do you desire and long for that which you neither know nor see?
Being thus questioned, he would answer: “Yes.”
“What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda?
When that is the case, does not the speech of that man turn out to be without foundation?
“Certainly, Bhante, when that is the case, the speech of that man turns out to be without foundation.”
“In the same way, Poṭṭhapāda, when those ascetics and brahmins hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
‘The self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death,’ I approach them and say this:”

‘Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a doctrine and such a view as this: “The self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death”? If, when asked thus by me, they admit, ‘It is so,’ then I say to them: ‘But, venerable sirs, do you know for certain that the self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death? When asked thus, they say, ‘No. ‘But, venerable sirs, have you seen a self that is exclusively happy and free from disease after death? When asked thus, they say, ‘No. ‘But, venerable sirs, do you know of a path or a method by which one could know or see that the self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death? When asked thus, they say, ‘No. ‘Then, venerable sirs, since you do not know for certain, nor have you seen it, nor do you know of a path or method by which one could know or see it, it is clear that you assert what is unestablished and maintain a view based on mere faith. Thus I spoke, and those wanderers said to me: “Venerable Nāgasena, the Blessed One has said: ‘Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What are the four? The person who is boundless like space; the person who is like a great ocean; the person who is like a small pool; and the person who is like a shallow puddle. Of these, the person who is like a shallow puddle is the least of the four. Now, venerable Nāgasena, we are like a shallow puddle among these four kinds of persons. We do not know for certain, nor have we seen it, nor do we know of a path or method by which one could know or see it, yet we still assert what is unestablished and maintain a view based on mere faith. I say this to them:
"But do you, venerable sirs, dwell knowing and seeing the world as exclusively pleasant?
Being asked thus, they say, "No."
I say this to them:
"Venerable sirs, do you perceive yourselves as experiencing absolute happiness for even one night, or one day, or half a night, or half a day?
When asked thus, they say, "No."
I say this to them:
"But do you, venerable sirs, know:
'This is the path, this is the way for the realization of an exclusively happy world'?"
Being asked thus, they say, "No.
I then say to them:
"But, venerable sirs, do you hear the voices of those deities who have been reborn in a world of exclusive happiness as they speak?"
“Are you, dear sirs, practicing rightly? Are you, dear sirs, practicing straightly for the realization of a world of absolute happiness?
For we too, dear sirs, having practiced in this way, have been reborn in a world of absolute happiness.
When asked thus, they say, “No.”
“What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda? When this is so, does not the speech of those ascetics and brahmins turn out to be without foundation?
“Certainly, Bhante, when this is so, the speech of those ascetics and brahmins turns out to be without foundation.
“Poṭṭhapāda, it is just as if a man were to build a ladder at a crossroads for the purpose of ascending to a palace.”
They would say to him: "O man,
do you know where that palace stands— toward which you are making a ladder for ascending—
that palace is in the eastern direction, or the southern direction, or the western direction, or the northern direction?"
"Is it high, low, or middling?
Being asked thus, he would say, "No.
Then they would say to him:
"O man, are you building a ladder for the ascent of that palace which you neither know nor see?
Being thus asked, he would say, "Yes.
What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda?
“But if this were so, would that man’s speech not turn out to be unconvincing?
“Certainly, venerable sir, if this were so, that man’s speech would turn out to be unconvincing.
“In the same way, Poṭṭhapāda, those recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:”
‘The self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death.
Having approached them, I say this:
‘Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a doctrine and such a view?’”
‘The self is exclusively happy and free from illness after death’?
If, when asked this by me, they acknowledge,
“Yes,” then I say to them:
“But do you, venerable sirs, dwell knowing and seeing the world as exclusively pleasant?
When asked this, they say, “No. To them I say:
"But do you, venerable sirs, perceive yourselves as experiencing exclusively happiness for one night or one day, or even for half a night or half a day?
When asked this, they say, "No. To them I say:
"But do you, venerable sirs, know this path, this way, for the realization of an exclusively happy world?
When asked thus, they say, "No. To them I say:
"Furthermore, Venerable Ones, do you hear the voices of those deities who have been reborn in a world of exclusive happiness, as they say:
'You have practiced well, dear sirs; you have practiced straightly, dear sirs, for the realization of a world of exclusive happiness;
for we too, dear sirs, having practiced thus, have been reborn in a world of exclusive happiness'?"
“Being asked thus, they say, ‘No.
What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda? Is it not the case that, this being so, the speech of those ascetics and brahmins turns out to be without foundation?
“Certainly, venerable sir, this being so, the speech of those ascetics and brahmins turns out to be without foundation.”
2.2. The Three Acquisitions of a Self:
“Poṭṭhapāda, there are these three acquisitions of a self for me:
the gross acquisition of a self, the mind-made acquisition of a self, and the formless acquisition of a self.”
And what, Poṭṭhapāda, is the gross acquisition of a self?
It is that which possesses form, consists of the four great elements, and subsists on physical food; this is the gross acquisition of a self.
What is the mind-made acquisition of a self?
Possessing form, mind-made, complete in all limbs and parts, with no faculty lacking—this is the acquisition of a self consisting of mind.
What is the acquisition of a formless self?
Being formless, consisting of perception—this is the acquisition of a formless self.
“Furthermore, Poṭṭhapāda, I teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of even this gross acquisition of a self:
‘By practicing thus, you will abandon defiling states, increase purifying states,
and having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom, you will enter upon and abide in that state.’”
It may be, Poṭṭhapāda, that you might think:
"Defiling states will be abandoned, purifying states will increase,
and having realized for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom, he will enter and dwell therein."
‘...and this dwelling is painful.
But it should not be viewed in this way, Poṭṭhapāda.
Defiled states will indeed be abandoned, and purifying states will increase, leading to the fulfillment of wisdom.
And having personally realized, through direct knowledge, the fullness [of this] in this very life, he will enter upon and abide in it;
there will be gladness, rapture, tranquility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and a pleasant dwelling.
Poṭṭhapāda, I also teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of the mind-made acquisition of a self:
‘By practicing in this way, the defiling states will be abandoned in you, the purifying states will increase,
and you will dwell having yourself realized through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom.
It may be, Poṭṭhapāda, that you might think thus:
‘Defiled states will be abandoned, purifying states will increase,
and having personally realized through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment, abundance, and perfection of wisdom, he will enter and dwell therein;
yet this dwelling is still painful.’
But it should not be viewed in this way, Poṭṭhapāda.
Defiled states will be abandoned and purifying states will increase;
and having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom, he will enter upon and abide in that state.
There will be gladness, rapture, tranquility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and a blissful dwelling.
Poṭṭhapāda, I also teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of the immaterial acquisition of a self:
‘For those who practice accordingly, defiling states will be abandoned and purifying states will increase.’
‘Having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and expansion of wisdom, you shall enter upon and abide therein.
Now, Poṭṭhapāda, it may be that you think:
‘Defiling states will be abandoned, purifying states will increase, and there will be the fulfillment of wisdom.’”
"And having realized for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life the full expansion [of the mind], he will enter upon and abide in it,
yet this is an unpleasant dwelling.
But, Poṭṭhapāda, you should not view it in this way.
Defiled states will be abandoned, and purifying states will increase;
having personally realized through direct knowledge the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom in this very life, he will enter and dwell therein,
experiencing joy, rapture, tranquility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and a state of bliss.
If, Poṭṭhapāda, they were to ask us:
"But what, friend, is that gross acquisition of a self for the abandoning of which you teach the Dhamma,
such that for those practicing accordingly, defiling states will be abandoned and states conducive to purification will increase?"
‘Having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom, you shall enter upon and abide in it’—
if we were asked this, we would answer them thus: ‘Friends,
this is that gross acquisition of a self for the abandoning of which we teach the Dhamma, and for those who have practiced accordingly…’”
‘Your defiling states will be abandoned, your purifying states will increase,
and having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom, you will enter upon and abide in that state.
If others, Poṭṭhapāda, were to ask us thus:
“But what, friends, is this mind-made acquisition of self for the abandoning of which you teach the Dhamma,
such that by practicing accordingly, defiling states will be abandoned in you, states conducive to purification will increase, and you,
having realized for yourselves with direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom, will enter and dwell therein?”
If we were asked this, we would answer thus:
"Friends, this is that mind-made acquisition of self for the abandoning of which we teach the Dhamma;
and for those of you who practice accordingly, defiling states will be abandoned, brightening states will increase, and there will be the fulfillment of wisdom."
‘and you will dwell having yourself realized through direct higher knowledge in this very life the fullness of that state.
If others, Poṭṭhapāda, were to ask us:
‘But which, friends, is that formless acquisition of self for the abandoning of which you teach the Dhamma?’”
‘If you practice in such a way, defiling states will be abandoned in you, brightening states will increase,
and you will dwell having personally realized through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom?
Being asked thus, we would answer them as follows:
‘Or this, friends, is that formless acquisition of a self for the abandoning of which we teach the Dhamma, such that by practicing accordingly,
defiling states will be abandoned in you and states conducive to purification will increase; and you,
having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom, will enter upon and abide in that state.’”
“What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda, when this is so,
does that statement not become something that possesses a basis for proof?
“Certainly, venerable sir, when this is so, that statement becomes something that possesses a basis for proof.”
“Just as if, Poṭṭhapāda, a man were to construct a ladder for ascending a palace, at the very base of that palace,
and someone were to say to him:
‘Good man, do you know that palace for which you are constructing a ladder for ascending?’”
‘In the eastern direction, or the southern direction, or the western direction, or the northern direction,
is there one who is tall, or short, or of medium height? He would say this:
‘Or, friend, this is that very palace for which I am making a ladder to ascend; it is right beneath that same palace.
What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda, does not the man’s speech in this case turn out to be authoritative?”
“Certainly, Bhante, if that were the case, then the speech of that man would indeed be supported by reason.
“In the same way, Poṭṭhapāda, if others were to ask us:
‘But what, friends, is that gross acquisition of a self? ... [and so on].”
"But what, friends, is that mind-made acquisition of self?

... And what, friends, is that formless acquisition of self, for the abandoning of which you teach the Dhamma, such that for those who practice accordingly, defiling states will be abandoned and states conducive to purification will increase?"
‘...will you dwell having realized for yourselves with direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom?
Being asked thus, we would answer them:
‘Friends, this is that formless acquisition of self for the abandoning of which we teach the Dhamma, and for those who have practiced accordingly—’”
‘Your defiling states will be abandoned, your purifying states will increase,
and you will dwell having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom.
What do you think, Poṭṭhapāda, would such a statement not be well-founded and authoritative?”
“Certainly, Bhante, when that is the case, what has been said becomes well-founded and authoritative.
When this was said, Citta Hatthisāriputta said to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, at whatever time there is a gross acquisition of a self, at that time the mind-made acquisition of a self is vain, and the formless acquisition of a self is vain.”
At that time, his gross acquisition of a self is real.
But, venerable sir, at whatever time there is an immaterial acquisition of a self, at that time his gross acquisition of a self is vain and his formless acquisition of a self is vain;
rather, at that time his mind-made acquisition of a self is real.
“Venerable sir, at whatever time there is an immaterial acquisition of self, at that time the gross acquisition of self is vain, and the mind-made acquisition of self is vain;
at that time, the immaterial acquisition of self is real.
“But, Citta, at whatever time there is a gross acquisition of self, at that time it is not reckoned as a mind-made acquisition of self, nor is it reckoned as an immaterial acquisition of self.”
At that time, it is reckoned simply as a gross acquisition of a self.
Citta, at whatever time there is an acquisition of a mind-made self, at that time it is neither reckoned as a gross acquisition of a self nor reckoned as a formless acquisition of a self;
at that time, it is reckoned simply as an acquisition of a mind-made self.
Citta, at whatever time there is an immaterial acquisition of self, at that time it is not reckoned as a gross acquisition of self, nor is it reckoned as a mind-made acquisition of self;
at that time it is reckoned simply as an immaterial acquisition of self.
Citta, if they were to ask you this:
‘In the past you existed, it is not that you did not exist;
in the future you will exist, it is not that you will not exist;
at present you exist, it is not that you do not exist.’
“If you were asked this, Citta, how would you answer?
“Venerable sir, if they were to ask me:
‘Did you exist in the past, or did you not exist?’”
‘In the future you will exist; it is not that you will not exist.
You exist now; it is not that you do not exist.
Being asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer thus:
‘I existed in the past, it is not that I did not exist;
I shall exist in the future, it is not that I shall not exist;
I exist now, it is not that I do not exist.’
“If I were asked this, Bhante, I would answer thus.
“But if they were to ask you, Citta:
‘That acquisition of a self which was yours in the past—that alone is your true acquisition of a self; the future one is vain, and the present one is vain—is that so?’”
“Whatever acquisition of a self you will have in the future, that alone would be your true acquisition of a self; the past would be vain, and the present would be vain.
Whatever acquisition of a self you have now in the present, that alone would be your true acquisition of a self; the past would be vain, and the future would be vain.
Being asked thus, Citta, how would you answer?”
“But if, venerable sir, they were to ask me thus:
‘That acquisition of a self which was yours in the past—that alone is your true acquisition of a self; the future is vain, the present is vain.
That acquisition of a self which will be yours in the future—that alone is your true acquisition of a self; the past is vain, the present is vain.’”
‘That acquisition of a self which you have now in the present is the only acquisition of a self that is real for you; the past was vain, and the future will be vain.
If I were asked this, Bhante, I would answer thus:
‘That acquisition of a self which I had in the past was the only acquisition of a self that was real at that time; the future was vain, and the present was vain.’”
‘Whatever acquisition of a self I may have in the future, that alone will be my true acquisition of a self at that time; the past will be vain, and the present will be vain.
Whatever acquisition of a self I have now in the present, that alone is my true acquisition of a self; the past will be vain, and the future will be vain.
Thus questioned, venerable sir, I would answer in this way.”

“In the same way, Citta, at whatever time there is a gross acquisition of self, at that time it is not reckoned as a mind-made acquisition of self, nor is it reckoned as a formless acquisition of self;
at that time it is reckoned simply as a gross acquisition of self.
At whatever time, Citta, there is a mind-made acquisition of self …” [and so on].
Citta, at whatever time there is an immaterial acquisition of self, at that time it is not reckoned as a gross acquisition of self, nor is it reckoned as a mind-made acquisition of self;
at that time it is simply reckoned as an immaterial acquisition of self.
Just as, Citta, from a cow comes milk, from milk curd, from curd butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee.
At the time when there is milk, at that time it is not reckoned as curd, nor is it reckoned as butter, nor is it reckoned as ghee, nor is it reckoned as the cream of ghee;
at that time it is reckoned simply as milk.
At the time when there is curd... [and so on].
When it becomes butter, when it becomes clarified butter,
and when it becomes the cream of clarified butter, at that time it is no longer reckoned as milk, nor is it reckoned as curd, nor is it reckoned as butter, nor is it reckoned as clarified butter.
At that time, it is reckoned as the cream of ghee.
In the same way, Citta, at whatever time there is a gross acquisition of a self...
[as before] ...at whatever time, Citta, there is a mind-made acquisition of a self... [as before] ...
"Citta, at whatever time there is an immaterial acquisition of self, at that time it is not reckoned as a gross acquisition of self, nor is it reckoned as a mind-made acquisition of self;
at that time it is reckoned simply as an immaterial acquisition of self.
These, Citta, are the worldly designations, the worldly expressions, the worldly conventions, and the worldly descriptions by which a Tathāgata speaks without misapprehending them."
When this was said, the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda said to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or one who might show the way, or might hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with sight might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been elucidated by the Blessed One in many ways.
Therefore, venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
Then Citta Hatthisāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!

Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—[even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One].”
"In this very way, the Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many methods.
Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, venerable sir; may I receive full ordination."
Citta Hatthisāriputta received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.

Not long after his full ordination, the venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time attained that goal for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
He went forth, and having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life—the end of the spiritual path—he dwelt therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta became one of the Arahants.
The Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, the ninth, is finished.
